subject: physics

items.q: A torch is left switched on until its battery is flat. What has happened to the energy that was in the chemical store of the battery?
items.correct: It has been transferred to light and to thermal stores, so the total is unchanged.
items.misconception: It has slowly been used up, so there is less energy now than at the start.
items.why: Everyday language talks about a battery 'running out' of energy, and the useful effect really does stop, so the energy appears to have gone. Energy cannot be created or destroyed. The chemical store of the battery has emptied, but exactly the same total energy is now spread through the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: The part of it that was wasted has been destroyed inside the torch.

items.q: A ball bearing rolls along a bench and slowly comes to rest. The ball, the bench and the surrounding air are treated as a closed system. What is true of the total energy of this system?
items.correct: It is unchanged; the kinetic store has emptied into the thermal stores.
items.misconception: It has fallen, because friction has let some of the energy leak out of it.
items.why: Students meet friction as something that 'takes energy away' and do not notice that the thermal stores it fills are inside the boundary of the closed system. In a closed system nothing crosses the boundary. The energy has moved from the kinetic store to the thermal stores of the ball, the surface and the air, all of which are inside the system.
items.random_wrong: It has fallen, because energy was used up in slowing the ball down.

items.q: In every system change some of the energy is dissipated. What does dissipated mean?
items.correct: The energy is stored in less useful ways, usually in thermal stores.
items.misconception: The energy is stored in the surroundings and later returns to the system.
items.why: Students are told that energy is never lost, and reason that anything which has not been destroyed must still be available for use. Conservation says the energy still exists, not that it is still useful. Once dissipated it is shared among a huge number of particles at a temperature close to that of the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: The energy is shared out equally between all the stores in the system.

items.q: A food mixer is running. Which energy transfer in the mixer is best described as ‘wasted’?
items.correct: The transfer to the thermal store of the warm motor.
items.misconception: The transfer that is destroyed by friction in the bearings.
items.why: Wasted energy cannot be collected and reused, and it becomes impossible to detect once it is spread thinly, so students equate 'cannot be used' with 'no longer exists'. Dissipated energy is still there; it has simply been spread so thinly through the surroundings that it can no longer do anything useful.
items.random_wrong: The transfer to the kinetic store of the rotating blades.

items.q: The bearings of a machine are oiled regularly. Why does this reduce the unwanted energy transfers?
items.correct: There is less friction, so less energy is dissipated to the thermal stores.
items.misconception: The oil takes in the wasted energy and stores it so it can be used again.
items.why: Students are told that energy is never lost, and reason that anything which has not been destroyed must still be available for use. Conservation says the energy still exists, not that it is still useful. Once dissipated it is shared among a huge number of particles at a temperature close to that of the surroundings.
items.random_wrong: The oil removes the friction entirely, so no energy is dissipated.

items.q: Thick insulation is laid in the loft of a house. Which statement about the house is now correct?
items.correct: The building now cools down more slowly than it did before.
items.misconception: No energy can leave through the loft now, so the house never cools.
items.why: The word 'insulator' is heard as an absolute barrier, like a waterproof coat, rather than as something that slows a rate. Insulation reduces the rate of transfer; it does not stop it. An insulated house still cools, just more slowly than an uninsulated one.
items.random_wrong: The insulation gives out warmth of its own and heats the rooms up.

items.q: Two saucepan handles are the same size and shape, but one is made from a material with a higher thermal conductivity than the other. Which statement about that handle is correct?
items.correct: It transfers energy by conduction at a higher rate than the other one.
items.misconception: It transfers energy more slowly, because it holds the energy inside itself.
items.why: The word 'conductivity' is read as a measure of how much energy the material can keep, and 'high' is assumed to be good. The higher the thermal conductivity, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material. Good insulators have a low thermal conductivity.
items.random_wrong: It transfers energy at the same rate, as the handles match in size.

items.q: Two houses are identical except that one has thicker outside walls, built from the same brick. On a cold night, compared with the other house, the house with the thicker walls will
items.correct: cool down more slowly than the house with thinner walls.
items.misconception: cool down faster, because there is more brick that has to be warmed up.
items.why: Students correctly recall that more mass needs more energy to warm it, then apply that idea to the wrong quantity, the rate of transfer out of the building. The extra brick does have to be warmed, but the question is about the rate at which energy crosses the wall, and that rate falls as the wall gets thicker.
items.random_wrong: cool at the same rate, because the brick has the same conductivity.

items.q: An architect wants a new building to cool down as slowly as possible on a cold night. Which change should be made to its walls?
items.correct: Make them thicker and use a material of lower thermal conductivity.
items.misconception: Build them from a material that has a higher thermal conductivity.
items.why: The word 'conductivity' is read as a measure of how much energy the material can keep, and 'high' is assumed to be good. The higher the thermal conductivity, the higher the rate of energy transfer by conduction across the material. Good insulators have a low thermal conductivity.
items.random_wrong: Make them thinner so that less brick has to be warmed up first.

items.q: In required practical activity 2, identical beakers of hot water are wrapped in different materials and the water temperature is recorded for ten minutes. Which result identifies the best insulator?
items.correct: The beaker whose water fell in temperature by the smallest amount.
items.misconception: The beaker whose water fell in temperature by the largest amount of all.
items.why: Students look for the biggest number in the results table and assume that the biggest change means the best performance. A good insulator slows the transfer out of the beaker, so the water stays hot. The smallest temperature drop identifies the best insulator.
items.random_wrong: The beaker whose water was the hottest when the timing started.

items.q: A student investigates how the thickness of an insulating layer affects the cooling of hot water in a beaker. Which measurements should be taken?
items.correct: The thickness of the layer, and the water temperature at set times.
items.misconception: The temperature of the water at the end of the run, and nothing else.
items.why: The final reading answers 'how hot is it now', so students treat the readings taken along the way as unnecessary. Cooling is a rate, so temperature must be recorded against time. AT 1 and AT 5 require appropriate apparatus for measuring length, temperature and time.
items.random_wrong: The temperature of the room, measured at the start and again at the end.

items.q: The student repeats the cooling run three times for each material and calculates a mean temperature drop. Why is this done?
items.correct: To reduce the effect of random error and give a more reliable result.
items.misconception: So that the water is given more time in which to cool down properly.
items.why: The first result looks like a perfectly good number, and the point of repeating is not visible unless the readings differ. Single readings scatter because of small random variations. Repeating and taking a mean reduces that scatter and lets anomalous results be spotted.
items.random_wrong: To make every material finish at the same final temperature.

items.q: A small electric motor is supplied with 800 J of energy. Of this, 260 J is transferred usefully to a kinetic store. What is the efficiency of the motor?
items.why: Students remember that the equation is a fraction made from two energies but not which one goes on top, and dividing the bigger by the smaller feels safer. The useful output goes on top. Dividing the input by the output gives a number greater than 1, which cannot be an efficiency.

items.q: Which statement about the efficiency of a device is correct?
items.correct: The efficiency of a device can never be greater than 1.
items.misconception: A very well made device can have an efficiency of more than 1.
items.why: Percentages above 100% are common in everyday talk about improvement, and students do not connect efficiency back to conservation of energy. Energy cannot be created, so the useful output is at most equal to the input. Efficiency therefore lies between 0 and 1, or between 0% and 100%.
items.random_wrong: Efficiency is measured in joules when energy values are used.

items.q: A motor has a total power input of 1200 W and a useful power output of 900 W. What is the efficiency of the motor?
items.why: Students remember that the equation is a fraction made from two energies but not which one goes on top, and dividing the bigger by the smaller feels safer. The useful output goes on top. Dividing the input by the output gives a number greater than 1, which cannot be an efficiency.

items.q: (HT) A gearbox wastes energy because of friction between its moving parts. Which change would increase the efficiency of the intended energy transfer?
items.correct: Lubricate the moving parts to reduce the energy dissipated.
items.misconception: Supply more power to the gearbox, so that it does more work each second.
items.why: Students associate 'more powerful' with 'better', and efficiency is assumed to be another word for performance. Efficiency is a ratio. Increasing the input raises the output as well, so the ratio barely changes; only cutting the wasted share raises efficiency.
items.random_wrong: Remove the friction completely so the gearbox is 100% efficient.

items.q: What does oiling the bearings of a machine do?
items.correct: It lowers the friction between the moving surfaces, so less energy is dissipated as the machine runs.
items.misconception: Oil removes friction completely, so a lubricated machine dissipates no energy at all.
items.why: Oiled parts feel effortless to turn, and textbook problems often describe smooth surfaces as 'frictionless'. Lubrication reduces friction, it does not abolish it. Some energy is still dissipated to thermal stores, which is why no real machine is 100% efficient.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does a room feel warmer after insulation is fitted?
items.correct: The energy from the heating stays in the room for longer, because it is transferred out more slowly.
items.misconception: The insulation gives out warmth of its own, which is why insulated rooms feel warmer.
items.why: Insulating materials such as wool feel warm to the touch, because they conduct energy away from the skin only slowly. Insulation is not an energy source. It has no store to empty; it simply slows the transfer of energy out of the room.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two walls are built from the same brick, one thicker than the other. How do they compare?
items.correct: They have the same thermal conductivity, but the thicker wall transfers energy at a lower rate.
items.misconception: The thicker wall has a lower thermal conductivity, and that is why thick walls keep a building warm.
items.why: Thickness and conductivity both change the rate of transfer, so students merge the two into a single property of the wall. Thermal conductivity is a property of the material alone. Thickness is a separate factor: for the same material, a thicker wall gives a lower rate of transfer.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What must be kept the same when different insulating materials are compared?
items.correct: The volume and starting temperature of the water, the container, the room and the time allowed.
items.misconception: Only the material matters; the volume of water and its starting temperature can be left to vary.
items.why: Students focus on the variable being investigated and forget that any other difference also changes the amount of cooling. Only the insulating material should differ. If the volume or the starting temperature changes as well, the comparison between the materials is no longer valid.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What makes the comparison between materials fair in this practical?
items.correct: Every beaker starts at the same temperature and is left for the same length of time.
items.misconception: To be fair, every material should be made to finish at the same final temperature.
items.why: 'Fair test' is remembered as 'make everything the same', which is then applied to the outcome as well as to the conditions. The final temperature is the result, so it must be free to differ. What must be kept the same are the starting conditions and the time allowed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does the efficiency of a device tell you?
items.correct: The share of the input energy transfer that ends up in the useful output.
items.misconception: Efficiency gives the fraction of the input energy that is wasted.
items.why: Lessons about efficiency dwell on wasted energy, so students attach the number to the waste rather than to the useful output. Efficiency counts the useful output. The wasted fraction is what is left over, so an efficiency of 0.3 means that 0.7 of the input is dissipated.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What unit does efficiency have?
items.correct: None. Efficiency is a ratio of two energies, or of two powers, so the units cancel.
items.misconception: Efficiency is measured in joules when energies are used, and in watts when powers are used.
items.why: Every other quantity in the topic carries a unit, and the numbers substituted into the equation are in joules or in watts. Dividing joules by joules, or watts by watts, leaves a pure number. Efficiency is written as a decimal or as a percentage, with no unit.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a machine be made 100% efficient?
items.correct: No real machine is. Some energy is always dissipated, so efficiency can be raised but never reaches 1.
items.misconception: A machine that is oiled and insulated well enough wastes nothing and becomes 100% efficient.
items.why: Every method taught for improving efficiency reduces waste, so students extrapolate to a machine that wastes nothing at all. Friction and temperature differences can be reduced but not removed, so there is always some dissipation in a working machine.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.1.2 Conservation and dissipation of energy
